question_html: What is the primary purpose of admitting a new partner into a partnership firm?

options.A: To dissolve the existing firm legally
options.B: For increasing the partnership capital or for strengthening the management of the firm
options.C: To reduce the tax liability of old partners to zero
options.D: To change the legal status of the firm into a public limited company

answer_html: Answer: (B) New partners are admitted either for increasing the partnership capital or for strengthening the management of the firm[cite: 22].
topic_text: Introduction to Admission of a Partner

question_html: What is another name for the Revaluation Account?

options.A: Realisation Account

answer_html: Answer: (B) A Revaluation Account is also known as a Profit and Loss Adjustment Account[cite: 22].

question_html: To which account is the profit or loss on revaluation transferred upon the admission of a new partner?

options.A: Capital accounts of all partners in the new profit-sharing ratio
options.B: Capital accounts of old partners in the old profit-sharing ratio

answer_html: Answer: (B) The profit or loss on revaluation is transferred to the Capital Accounts of old partners in the old profit sharing ratio[cite: 22].

question_html: How should general reserves appearing in the balance sheet be treated on the admission of a new partner?

options.A: Transferred to the capital accounts of old partners in their old profit sharing ratio
options.B: Carried forward unchanged in the new balance sheet without adjustment
options.C: Distributed among all partners including the new partner in the new profit sharing ratio
options.D: Transferred entirely to the Revaluation Account

answer_html: Answer: (A) Whenever a new partner is admitted, any reserve appearing in the Balance Sheet should be transferred to the Capital Accounts of the old partners in the old profit sharing ratio[cite: 22].

question_html: What is the sacrificing ratio formula?

options.A: New Profit Sharing Ratio minus Old Profit Sharing Ratio
options.B: Old Profit Sharing Ratio minus New Profit Sharing Ratio
options.C: Old Profit Sharing Ratio plus New Profit Sharing Ratio
options.D: Capital Contribution Ratio divided by two

answer_html: Answer: (B) Sacrificing ratio = Old Profit sharing ratio minus New Profit sharing ratio[cite: 22].

question_html: When a new partner is admitted and the question is silent about how the old partners sacrifice their shares, what is the default assumption?

options.A: Old partners sacrifice equally regardless of old ratio
options.B: Old partners sacrifice in their old profit sharing ratio

answer_html: Answer: (B) When the question is silent about the sacrifice made by old partners, it is assumed that old partners share the remaining share in their old profit sharing ratio, which makes their sacrificing ratio equal to their old ratio[cite: 22].
topic_text: Computation of New Profit Sharing Ratio

question_html: How many parts does a Memorandum Revaluation Account have?

options.A: One part

answer_html: Answer: (B) Memorandum revaluation account has two parts: the first part for old partners and the second part for all partners including the new partner[cite: 22].

question_html: In the first part of a Memorandum Revaluation Account, the profit or loss on revaluation is transferred to:

options.A: All partners in the new profit sharing ratio
options.B: Old partners only in their old profit sharing ratio

answer_html: Answer: (B) The resultant profit or loss on revaluation in the first part of the Memorandum Revaluation Account is transferred to the capital accounts of old partners only in the old profit and loss sharing ratio[cite: 22].

question_html: What happens to the book values of assets and liabilities when a Memorandum Revaluation Account is used?

options.A: They are changed to their current market fair values in the balance sheet
options.B: They remain unchanged at their old book values in the balance sheet
options.C: They are written down to zero

answer_html: Answer: (B) When a Memorandum Revaluation Account is prepared, the book values of assets and liabilities do not change and appear in the new balance sheet at their old figures[cite: 22].

question_html: How is hidden or inferred goodwill calculated when not explicitly given?

options.A: Incoming partner's capital multiplied by the reciprocal of their share, minus total capital of old partners plus net accumulated profits/reserves and incoming capital
options.B: Average profit multiplied by years of purchase
options.C: Total assets minus total outside liabilities
options.D: Revaluation profit divided by old profit sharing ratio

answer_html: Answer: (A) Hidden goodwill is calculated as (Incoming partner's capital $ imes$ Reciprocal of share) minus (Total capital of old partners + Net Accumulated Profits and Reserves + Capital brought in by incoming partner)[cite: 22].

question_html: When an asset's value increases upon revaluation at the time of admission, how is it recorded in a standard Revaluation Account?

options.A: Debited to Revaluation Account
options.C: Credited to Partners' Current Accounts directly

answer_html: Answer: (B) An increase in the value of an asset represents a gain and is credited to the Revaluation Account[cite: 22].

question_html: When a liability increases upon reassessment at the time of admission, how is it recorded?

options.A: Debited to Revaluation Account
options.C: Debited to Incoming Partner's Capital Account
options.D: Credited to Trade Payables Account only without Revaluation

answer_html: Answer: (A) An increase in liability is a loss and is debited to the Revaluation Account[cite: 22].

question_html: Do newly admitted partners have the same rights as old partners by default?

options.A: No, they have no voting or profit rights ever
options.B: Yes, all partners have the same rights at all times unless contrary is provided in the partnership deed or agreed by partners
options.C: Only after completing 5 years in the firm
options.D: Only if they contribute double the capital

answer_html: Answer: (B) All the partners have the same rights at all times, unless a contrary provision is made in the partnership deed or agreed by the partners[cite: 22].

question_html: Is a newly admitted partner entitled to share in reserves appearing in the balance sheet prior to their admission?

options.A: Yes, equally with all partners
options.B: No, such reserves belong to old partners in their old profit sharing ratio
options.C: Yes, in their new profit sharing ratio
options.D: Only if the new partner pays extra cash for reserves

answer_html: Answer: (B) A new partner is not entitled to have any share in the reserves of the firm prior to admission; such reserves are distributed to old partners in their old profit sharing ratio[cite: 22].

question_html: In the second part of a Memorandum Revaluation Account, the balance representing the reversal effect is transferred to:

options.A: Old partners only in old ratio
options.B: All partners including the new partner in the new profit sharing ratio

answer_html: Answer: (B) The balance of the second part of the Memorandum Revaluation Account is transferred to all partners including the new partner in the new profit and loss sharing ratio[cite: 22].

question_html: A and B are partners sharing profits and losses in the ratio 5:3. They admitted C and agreed to give him 3/10th of the profit. If C acquires his share by taking 1/5th from A and 1/10th from B, what is the new profit sharing ratio?
answer_html: Answer: (C) A's new share = 5/8 - 1/5 = (25-8)/40 = 17/40 = 34/80; B's new share = 3/8 - 1/10 = (15-4)/40 = 11/40 = 22/80; C's share = 3/10 = 24/80. Ratio is 34:22:24 or simplified to 17:11:12 (or matching study material test your knowledge MCQ 2 option C)[cite: 22].

question_html: C was admitted in a firm with 1/4th share of the profits. C contributes ₹15,000 as his capital. A and B are other partners with a profit sharing ratio of 3:2. If capital should be in profit sharing ratio taking C's capital as the base, what are the required capitals of A and B?
answer_html: Answer: (B) Total capital of the firm based on C = ₹15,000 $ imes$ 4 = ₹60,000. A's capital = ₹60,000 $ imes$ (3/5) = ₹36/1? Wait, let's check: if C is 1/4th, remaining 3/4th is shared between A and B in 3:2. A = 3/4 $ imes$ 3/5 = 9/20 $ imes$ 60,000 = ₹27,000; B = 3/4 $ imes$ 2/5 = 6/20 $ imes$ 60,000 = ₹18,000[cite: 22].

question_html: A, B and C are partners sharing profits and losses in the ratio 6:3:3. They agreed to take D into partnership for 1/8th share of profits. What is the new profit sharing ratio?

A and B are partners sharing profits and losses in the ratio of 3:2 (A's Capital is ₹30,000 and B's Capital is ₹15,000). They admitted C and agreed to give 1/5th share of profits to him. How much should C bring in towards his capital if capital is based on proportionate combined capital of old partners?
answer_html: Answer: (C) Combined capital of A and B = ₹30,000 + ₹15,000 = ₹45,000. This represents 4/5th share (1 - 1/5). Total capital of the firm = ₹45,000 $ imes$ (5/4) = ₹56,250. C's capital for 1/5th share = ₹56,250 $ imes$ (1/5) = ₹11,250[cite: 22].

question_html: X and Y are partners sharing profits in the ratio of 3:1. They admit Z as a partner who pays ₹4,000 as goodwill, the new profit sharing ratio being 2:1:1 among X, Y and Z respectively. To whom will the amount of goodwill be credited?

options.A: X and Y as ₹3,000 and ₹1,000 respectively
options.D: Equally between X, Y and Z

answer_html: Answer: (B) Sacrificing ratio: X = 3/4 - 2/4 = 1/4; Y = 1/4 - 1/4 = 0. Since only X sacrifices his share, the entire goodwill premium is credited to X[cite: 22].

question_html: P and Q are partners sharing profits in the ratio of 2:1. R is admitted with effect from 1st April on the term that he will bring ₹20,000 as capital for 1/4th share and pays ₹9,000 for goodwill, half of which is withdrawn by P and Q. Opening capital of P is ₹40,000, Q is ₹30,000, and revaluation profit is ₹6,000. What is the closing balance of P's capital?
answer_html: Answer: (A) P's capital = Opening ₹40,000 + Revaluation profit (2/3 of ₹6,000 = ₹4,000) + Goodwill share (2/3 of ₹9,000 = ₹6,000) - Withdrawal (half of share = ₹3,000) = ₹40,000 + ₹4,000 + ₹6,000 - ₹3,000 = ₹47,000[cite: 22].

question_html: Adam, Brain and Chris were equal partners with goodwill ₹1,20,000 shown in the balance sheet. They agreed to take Daniel as an equal partner on the term that he should bring ₹1,60,000 as capital, and his share of goodwill was evaluated at ₹60,000. If the existing goodwill account is to be written off before admission, what is the correct treatment?

options.A: Write off existing goodwill of ₹1,20,000 in old ratio and distribute Daniel's goodwill in sacrificing ratio
options.C: Ignore existing goodwill and record only Daniel's goodwill
options.D: Capitalize all goodwill in the new ratio

answer_html: Answer: (A) Existing goodwill appearing in the balance sheet must be written off among old partners in the old ratio, and goodwill brought in/valued for the new partner is adjusted via sacrificing ratio[cite: 22].

question_html: A and B are partners sharing profits in 3:2. C is admitted for 1/3rd share which he gets 1/9th from A and 2/9th from B. What is the new profit sharing ratio?
A and B are partners sharing in 3:2. A surrenders 1/3rd of his share and B surrenders 2/3rd of his share in favour of C. What is the new profit sharing ratio?
answer_html: Answer: (A) A's surrender = 3/5 $ imes$ 1/3 = 3/15; A's new share = 3/5 - 3/15 = 6/15. B's surrender = 2/5 $ imes$ 2/3 = 4/15; B's new share = 2/5 - 4/15 = 2/15. C's share = 3/15 + 4/15 = 7/15. New ratio = 6:2:7[cite: 22].

question_html: A and B are partners sharing profits in 3:2. C is admitted for 1/5th share which he acquires from A and B in the ratio of 2:1. What is the new profit sharing ratio?
answer_html: Answer: (A) A's sacrifice = 1/5 $ imes$ 2/3 = 2/15; A's new share = 3/5 - 2/15 = 7/15. B's sacrifice = 1/5 $ imes$ 1/3 = 1/15; B's new share = 2/5 - 1/15 = 5/15. C's share = 1/5 $ imes$ 3/3 = 3/15. New ratio = 7:5:3[cite: 22].

question_html: X and Y are partners sharing profits and losses in the ratio 5:3. They admit Z, and the new ratio becomes 3:2:1. What is the sacrificing ratio of X and Y?
answer_html: Answer: (A) X's sacrifice = 5/8 - 3/6 = (15 - 12)/24 = 3/24; Y's sacrifice = 3/8 - 2/6 = (9 - 8)/24 = 1/24. Sacrificing ratio = 3:1[cite: 22].

question_html: A and B are partners with capitals of ₹7,000 each. They admit C as a partner with 1/4th share in profits. C brings ₹8,000 as his share of capital. What is the hidden goodwill of the firm and C's share of goodwill?

options.A: Firm goodwill ₹10,000; C's share ₹2,500

answer_html: Answer: (A) Total capital based on C = ₹8,000 $ imes$ 4 = ₹32,000. Actual combined capital = ₹7,000 + ₹7,000 + ₹8,000 = ₹22,000. Hidden goodwill = ₹32,000 - ₹22,000 = ₹10,000. C's share = ₹10,000 $ imes$ (1/4) = ₹2,500[cite: 22].

question_html: A and B are partners sharing profits in 3:2. They admit C for 1/6th share who introduces ₹25,000 capital. New ratio is 3:2:1. If C is unable to bring goodwill in cash and goodwill is calculated based on C's capital contribution, what is the hidden goodwill of the firm?
answer_html: Answer: (A) Total capital of firm based on C = ₹25,000 $ imes$ 6 = ₹1,50,000. Combined capital of A, B, and C = ₹44,000 + ₹36,000 + ₹25,000 = ₹1,05,000. Hidden goodwill = ₹1,50,000 - ₹1,05,000 = ₹45,000[cite: 22].

question_html: In question 28, what is A's share of goodwill to be credited to A's capital account?
answer_html: Answer: (A) Sacrificing ratio of A: New share 3/6, Old share 3/5. Sacrifice = 3/5 - 3/6 = 3/30. A's share of goodwill = ₹45,000 $ imes$ (3/30) = ₹4,500[cite: 22].

question_html: A and B share profits in 3/4th and 1/4th proportion. C is admitted for 1/3rd share of profits, purchasing 1/3rd of goodwill for ₹2,000 and providing ₹10,000 as capital. Goodwill does not appear in books. What is total firm goodwill?
answer_html: Answer: (A) Since C pays ₹2,000 for 1/3rd share of goodwill, total goodwill of the firm = ₹2,000 $ imes$ 3 = ₹6,000[cite: 22].

question_html: A, B and C are partners sharing profits in 3:2:1 ratio. They change ratio to 2:2:1 or admit X, etc. In a case where X LLP admits X for 1/3rd share with ₹25,000 capital and ₹15,000 premium for goodwill (old ratio 3:2), revaluation loss is ₹8,250. What is A's share of revaluation loss?
answer_html: Answer: (A) Total revaluation loss = ₹8,250. Shared in old ratio 3:2. A's share = ₹8,250 $ imes$ (3/5) = ₹4,950[cite: 22].

question_html: In an LLP admission where Guru is admitted with 40% profit share, bringing ₹1,00,000 capital and goodwill valued at 2 years' purchase of 3 years' normal average profits (which equals ₹60,000 total firm goodwill), how much goodwill should Guru bring in cash?
answer_html: Answer: (A) Guru's share of goodwill = ₹60,000 $ imes$ 40% = ₹24,000[cite: 22].

question_html: If the net profit for the year ended 31.3.2020 is ₹20,000 which includes an abnormal insurance claim received of ₹40,000, what is the normal adjusted profit for that year for goodwill valuation?

options.A: Loss of ₹20,000

answer_html: Answer: (A) Normal adjusted profit = ₹20,000 - ₹40,000 (abnormal gain deducted) = -₹20,000 (Loss of ₹20,000)[cite: 22].

question_html: If a loss of ₹80,000 for the year ended 31.3.2021 includes a voluntary retirement compensation paid of ₹1,10,000 (an abnormal/non-recurring expense), what is the adjusted normal profit/loss for that year?

options.A: Profit of ₹30,000

answer_html: Answer: (A) Adjusted normal profit = -₹80,000 + ₹1,10,000 (adding back abnormal expense) = Profit of ₹30,000[cite: 22].

question_html: Dalal, Banerji and Mallick share profits in 2:2:1. Mr. Mistri is admitted with 2/15th share, and new ratio is 5:15, 5:15, 3:15, 2:15. What is the sacrificing ratio of Dalal and Banerji?
answer_html: Answer: (A) Dalal sacrifice = 2/5 - 5/15 = 1/15; Banerji sacrifice = 2/5 - 5/15 = 1/15. Sacrificing ratio is 1:1[cite: 22].

question_html: Leena and Meena share profits 2:3. General reserve is ₹40,000. On Neena's admission for 1/5th share, how is the general reserve distributed?

options.A: Leena ₹16,000; Meena ₹24,000
options.D: Distributed equally among all three partners

answer_html: Answer: (A) General reserve belongs to old partners in old ratio (2:3). Leena = ₹40,000 $ imes$ 2/5 = ₹16,000; Meena = ₹40,000 $ imes$ 3/5 = ₹24,000[cite: 22].

question_html: Alpha and Beeta share profits equally in Meta-Chem LLP. Gyama is admitted with 1/6th share. New profit sharing ratio is 3:2:1. What is Beeta's sacrifice or gain?

options.A: Sacrifice of 1/6th

answer_html: Answer: (A) Beeta's old share = 1/2 (or 3/6); new share = 2/6. Difference = 3/6 - 2/6 = 1/6 (sacrifice)[cite: 22].

question_html: In an admission where old partners' capitals are adjusted based on the new partner's capital and new profit-sharing ratio, if the required capital of a partner is less than their existing capital after revaluation and reserves, what is the accounting treatment?

options.A: Excess capital is withdrawn in cash by the partner
options.B: Excess capital is transferred to Revaluation Account
options.C: Excess capital is written off as bad debt
options.D: Excess capital remains untouched as a liability

answer_html: Answer: (A) Excess capital is withdrawn in cash by the partners to make capitals proportionate[cite: 22].

question_html: What is the key difference between Revaluation Account and Memorandum Revaluation Account regarding the Balance Sheet?

options.A: Revaluation Account shows assets/liabilities at revalued figures in the new balance sheet, whereas Memorandum Revaluation Account shows them at old figures
options.B: Memorandum Revaluation Account alters asset values permanently in ledger accounts
options.C: Revaluation Account is divided into two parts while Memorandum is not
options.D: There is no difference in balance sheet presentation

answer_html: Answer: (A) Revaluation account results in assets and liabilities appearing at revalued figures in the new balance sheet, whereas memorandum revaluation account keeps them at old figures[cite: 22].

question_html: A and B are partners sharing profits in 3:2. C is admitted for 1/5th share. What is the new profit sharing ratio?
answer_html: Answer: (A) Remaining share = 1 - 1/5 = 4/5. A = 4/5 $ imes$ 3/5 = 12/25; B = 4/5 $ imes$ 2/5 = 8/25; C = 1/5 = 5/25. Ratio = 12:8:5[cite: 22].
topic_text: New Profit Sharing Ratio Case I

question_html: If a Revaluation Account shows a credit balance, what does it signify and how is it treated?

options.A: It represents profit and is credited to old partners' capital accounts in their old profit sharing ratio
options.B: It represents loss and is debited to old partners equally
options.C: It is transferred to the new partner's capital account
options.D: It represents general reserve and is distributed to all partners

answer_html: Answer: (A) A credit balance in the Revaluation Account represents profit, which is credited to the old partners' capital accounts in their old profit sharing ratio[cite: 22].

question_html: In Illustration 7 (X LLP), A and B share profits in 3:2. X is admitted for 1/3rd share, and A and B agree to share remaining 2/3rd equally (1:1). What is the new profit sharing ratio of A, B, and X?
answer_html: Answer: (A) A = 2/3 $ imes$ 1/2 = 1/3; B = 2/3 $ imes$ 1/2 = 1/3; X = 1/3. New ratio is equal proportion (1:1:1)[cite: 22].
topic_text: New Profit Sharing Ratio Equal Proportion

question_html: In Illustration 7, X pays ₹15,000 as premium for goodwill for 1/3rd share. What is the total valuation of goodwill of the firm and the sacrificing ratio of A and B?

options.A: Total goodwill ₹45,000; Sacrificing ratio 4:1

answer_html: Answer: (A) Total goodwill = ₹15,000 $ imes$ 3 = ₹45,000. Sacrificing ratio: A = 3/5 - 1/3 = 4/15; B = 2/5 - 1/3 = 1/15. Ratio = 4:1[cite: 22].
topic_text: Goodwill Valuation and Sacrificing Ratio Problem

question_html: Leena and Meena admit Neena for 1/5th share with ₹80,000 capital. Goodwill is valued at ₹1,00,000. How is Neena's share of goodwill adjusted among old partners (Leena and Meena sharing 2:3)?

options.A: Neena's share of goodwill (₹20,000) debited to Neena and credited to Leena (₹8,000) and Meena (₹12,000)
options.D: Paid in cash and retained as asset

answer_html: Answer: (A) Neena's share of goodwill = ₹1,00,000 $ imes$ (1/5) = ₹20,000, which is credited to old partners in their sacrificing (old) ratio 2:3 (Leena gets ₹8,000, Meena gets ₹12,000)[cite: 22].

question_html: In Illustration 10, total revaluation profit (Profit & Loss Adjustment Account) amounts to ₹20,000 (Building appreciation ₹30,000 minus total asset write-downs ₹10,000). How is this profit shared between Leena and Meena (ratio 2:3)?

options.A: Leena ₹8,000; Meena ₹12,000

answer_html: Answer: (A) Revaluation profit of ₹20,000 is distributed in 2:3 ratio: Leena = ₹20,000 $ imes$ 2/5 = ₹8,000; Meena = ₹20,000 $ imes$ 3/5 = ₹12,000[cite: 22].

question_html: In Meta-Chem LLP (Illustration 11), general reserve of ₹1,80,000 and workmen compensation fund of ₹60,000 (with no actual liability) are distributed between Alpha and Beeta (equal partners) on admission. What total amount is credited to each partner's capital account from these reserves/funds?
answer_html: Answer: (A) Total reserve/fund = ₹1,80,000 + ₹60,000 = ₹2,40,000. Shared equally between Alpha and Beeta = ₹1,20,000 each[cite: 22].

question_html: In Illustration 11, total revaluation profit is ₹1,40,000 (shared equally between Alpha and Beeta). What is the revaluation profit credited to Alpha?
answer_html: Answer: (A) Revaluation profit of ₹1,40,000 shared equally between Alpha and Beeta gives ₹70,000 to each[cite: 22].

question_html: When preparing a Memorandum Revaluation Account, if the first part shows a revaluation profit of ₹40,000, what must the second part show?

options.A: A revaluation loss of ₹40,000

answer_html: Answer: (A) If there is a profit in the first half of the Memorandum Revaluation Account, the later half must show a loss of the same amount to reverse the effect[cite: 22].

question_html: A and B are partners sharing profits in 3:2. They admit C with 1/5th share. C acquires his share entirely from A. What is the new profit sharing ratio?
answer_html: Answer: (A) A's new share = 3/5 - 1/5 = 2/5; B's share = 2/5; C's share = 1/5. New ratio = 2:2:1[cite: 22].

question_html: In a partnership admission, if goodwill is paid privately by the incoming partner to the old partners, what is the accounting entry passed in the books of the firm?

options.A: No entry is passed in the books of the firm
options.B: Debit Bank Account and Credit Goodwill Account
options.C: Debit Incoming Partner's Capital Account and Credit Old Partners' Capital Accounts
options.D: Debit Goodwill Account and Credit Old Partners' Capital Accounts

answer_html: Answer: (A) When goodwill is paid privately outside the firm, no entry is required in the books of accounts of the firm[cite: 21].
